cs:sports.title: Gridiron Data Structures
cs:sports.overview: Welcome to the data stadium, where every roster spot and play call runs like a data structure. You will line up arrays, chain linked lists, and call stacks, queues, hash tables, and search trees to march down the field. Master how each formation stores plays and how fast it scales.
cs:sports.summary: Arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, and binary search trees trade fast access for fast insertion, with Big-O describing how cost grows. Balanced and uncrowded organization keeps operations fast, while shifting, scanning chains, and degenerate lines make them slow.
cs:sports.limitation: Football suggests athletes adjust and hustle, but data structures do not improvise: contiguous shifts, pointer follows, hash collisions, and tree degeneration follow fixed memory rules, not effort or instinct.

boss.name: Super Bowl Mastermind
boss.intro: Fourth quarter, tied game, one final drive to prove you command every data structure on the field!

subtopics.name: Arrays
subtopics.lesson: Like assigned seats on the team bench, an array stores elements in contiguous memory. That layout lets you read any index in O(1) time because you can jump straight to it. But like inserting a player mid-bench, inserting in the middle is O(n) because later elements must shift to make room.
subtopics.analogy: A starting lineup packed shoulder-to-shoulder on the bench in numbered seats.

enemy.name: Bench Blitz
enemy.taunt: You can't shift past my defensive line!

subtopics.name: Linked Lists
subtopics.lesson: Like a chain of laterals, a linked list stores nodes that each hold a value and a pointer to the next node. If you already know a node, inserting after it is O(1) because you only relink a pointer. But finding an element is O(n) because you must follow the chain from the start.
subtopics.analogy: A lateral relay where each ball carrier holds the ball and points to the next carrier.

enemy.name: Lateral Hunter
enemy.taunt: I'll break your chain before you reach the end zone!

subtopics.name: Stacks and Queues
subtopics.lesson: Like reusing only the top wristband, a stack is last-in, first-out with push and pop at the top in O(1), used for the call stack and undo features. Like players entering a drill at the back and leaving at the front, a queue is first-in, first-out with enqueue at the back and dequeue at the front. Breadth-first search and printer queues use queues.
subtopics.analogy: A stack of play wristbands where you take only the top one, versus a tunnel line where players enter at the back and exit at the front.

enemy.name: Turnover Rush
enemy.taunt: First in, last out — I'll sack your snap count!

subtopics.name: Hash Tables
subtopics.lesson: Like assigning each audibled play to a wristband number, a hash table uses a hash function to map keys to array indices. That gives average O(1) insert, lookup and delete. Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing, and the table resizes when the load factor gets too high.
subtopics.analogy: A coordinator's wristband that turns each play name into a numbered slot.

enemy.name: Blitz Checker
enemy.taunt: I'll collide with your coverage and blow up the play!

subtopics.name: Binary Search Trees and Big-O
subtopics.lesson: Like choosing left or right based on size, a binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right. Search, insert and delete are O(log n) when the tree is balanced but O(n) when it degenerates into a line. Big-O notation describes how running time grows with input size, ignoring constant factors.
subtopics.analogy: A quarterback's read that goes left for smaller defenders and right for larger ones, plus a scouting report measuring how plays scale.

enemy.name: Cover Two Safety
enemy.taunt: Read left, read right — I'll trap you in a straight line!

O(n)

Because arrays push and pop only at the top

questions.explanation: Contiguous memory lets an array calculate the location of any index directly for O(1) reads.

O(n)

First-in, first-out with enqueue at the back and dequeue at the front

options: How running time grows with input size, ignoring constant factors

How collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing
How to push and pop at the top in O(1)
questions.explanation: Big-O describes growth with input size while ignoring constant factors.

bio:fantasy.title: Knights of the Living Citadel
bio:fantasy.overview: You are a knight sworn to defend the Living Citadel, which is the cell itself. From the throne-room nucleus to the dragon-fired mitochondria and the outer curtain wall, you must master how each hall keeps the realm alive to drive back the dark horde.
bio:fantasy.summary: Eukaryotic cells coordinate DNA control, protein forging, energy production, and selective transport to live and grow. Prokaryotic cells lack these inner chambers, while plant cells add a cellulose wall, chloroplasts, and a large central vacuole for extra support and photosynthesis.
bio:fantasy.limitation: Castles and dragons imply conscious planning and magic, but cells run on chemistry without knights giving orders; membranes, enzymes, and gradients follow physical laws, not loyalty, and organelles are microscopic and interconnected rather than separate castle rooms.

boss.name: Morgath the World-Ender
boss.intro: Morgath the World-Ender descends in black fire to burn the walls, silence the throne, and swallow the Citadel whole!

subtopics.name: Realms of Life: Prokaryotes and Command
subtopics.lesson: A eukaryotic citadel is like a great castle with walled chambers, while a prokaryotic raider camp is an open hut without inner walls. The castle throne room is the nucleus, which stores DNA and controls gene expression to rule the realm. Within it, the nucleolus works like a royal workshop that builds ribosome subunits for later use.
subtopics.analogy: An open goblin camp versus a walled castle with a throne room and inner workshops

enemy.name: Camp Goblin
enemy.taunt: My horde needs no castle or king to survive!

subtopics.name: The Smithy Row: Ribosomes, ER, and Golgi
subtopics.lesson: Protein crafting in the citadel works like a line of knight-smithies. Ribosomes translate mRNA into proteins, working free in the courtyard cytoplasm or mounted on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which folds proteins and ships them onward. Nearby the smooth ER forges lipids and neutralizes toxins, while the Golgi acts as master quartermaster that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins into vesicles for delivery.
subtopics.analogy: Knight-smithies forging blades, side-forges brewing oil, and a quartermaster crating goods

enemy.name: Rust Ogre
enemy.taunt: I will melt your forges and scatter your crates to the wind!

subtopics.name: Dragons and Dungeons: Energy and Cleanup
subtopics.lesson: Mighty dragons in the deep halls are the mitochondria, carrying out cellular respiration that turns glucose and oxygen into ATP for all knightly work, and they carry their own small scroll of DNA. The dungeons below are the lysosomes, where powerful enzymes digest worn-out parts and debris to keep the castle clean.
subtopics.analogy: Fire-dragons powering the castle lanterns and dungeon pits dissolving refuse

enemy.name: Crypt Wraith
enemy.taunt: Your fire fades and your halls will rot with refuse!

subtopics.name: Walls and Gates: Membrane and Passive Passage
subtopics.lesson: The citadel wall is the plasma membrane, a phospholipid bilayer studded with proteins that is selectively permeable, deciding who may pass. When travelers drift downhill through open gates or guided doorways without spending the kingdom's energy, that is passive transport such as diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion moving substances down their concentration gradient.
subtopics.analogy: A castle curtain wall with guarded posterns letting travelers drift downhill for free

enemy.name: Siege Troll
enemy.taunt: No wall can keep my horde out forever, little knight!

subtopics.name: Upstream Sieges and Elven Gardens
subtopics.lesson: Sometimes supplies must be hauled uphill against the flow, and the citadel spends ATP to drive active transport against the concentration gradient, as with the sodium-potassium pump. Plant-allied towers add extra elven craft: a strong cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a large central vacuole for storage and support.
subtopics.analogy: Hauling supplies uphill with dragon-fire energy and elven towers with bark walls and sun-catchers

enemy.name: Dark Sorcerer
enemy.taunt: My magic drags rivers uphill — your gardens will wither!

options: Golgi translating lipids into proteins in vesicles

options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum

options: Rough endoplasmic reticulum

questions.explanation: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles.

options: Storing DNA to control gene expression
Turning glucose and oxygen into ATP

questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, turning glucose and oxygen into ATP.

options: Chloroplast
Mitochondrion

questions.explanation: The plasma membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins.

options: Freely permeable to all substances
Impermeable to all substances
Selectively permeable

questions.prompt: Refugees drift downhill through the mountain passes without spending provisions. Which process moves substances down their concentration gradient without energy?
options: Protein synthesis by ribosomes
Cellular respiration
Passive transport by diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion

options: Cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and large central vacuole

Smooth ER, Golgi, and sodium-potassium pump
questions.explanation: Plant cells have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a large central vacuole.

bio:sports.title: Gridiron Cell Showdown
bio:sports.overview: Welcome to the cellular gridiron, where every cell runs like a pro football franchise. You will scout lean prokaryotic squads and fully staffed eukaryotic teams while learning how organelles run protein plays, power drives, and goal-line defense. Master the playbook to push from kickoff to championship.
bio:sports.summary: From DNA storage in the nucleus to protein translation by ribosomes, folding in the rough ER, and packaging in the Golgi, cells coordinate specialized organelles with energy from mitochondria. The selectively permeable plasma membrane controls transport, while plant cells add a cellulose wall, chloroplasts, and central vacuole and prokaryotes play without a nucleus or membrane-bound organelles.
bio:sports.limitation: Football teams choose plays, get tired, and guard yards, but organelles follow DNA instructions and chemistry without coaching, and membranes, diffusion, pumps, and photosynthesis work by gradients and enzymes, not by whistles or scoring.

boss.name: Gridiron Overlord
boss.intro: Fourth and goal with seconds left, the undefeated champion storms under the lights to test your entire cell playbook!

subtopics.name: Roster Check: Prokaryotes vs Eukaryotes
subtopics.lesson: Like football programs at different levels, cells come in two basic organizations. Prokaryotic cells, such as bacteria, play without a nucleus and without membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotic cells in plants, animals, and fungi run a bigger operation with both a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles to compartmentalize jobs.
subtopics.analogy: Comparing a small pickup flag-football squad with no coaching booth to a full NFL franchise with suites and specialized units

enemy.name: Blitz Rookie
enemy.taunt: No nucleus, no mercy — I'm blitzing your brain!

subtopics.name: Head Coach HQ: Nucleus and Protein Start
subtopics.lesson: The nucleus stores DNA and controls gene expression like a head coach holding the master playbook. Inside it, the nucleolus builds ribosome subunits. Ribosomes then translate mRNA into proteins, working free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum, which folds proteins and ships them onward.
subtopics.analogy: A coach's booth holding the playbook with an inner shop building players for the assembly line

enemy.name: Playbook Picker
enemy.taunt: I'm intercepting your gene playbook!

subtopics.name: Blocking and Equipment Crew: ER, Golgi, Lysosomes
subtopics.lesson: After the initial protein play, the smooth ER handles lipid production and toxin breakdown like trainers conditioning and detoxing players. The Golgi apparatus then modifies, sorts, and packages proteins into vesicles for delivery. Lysosomes act as the stadium cleanup crew, using enzymes to digest worn-out parts and debris.
subtopics.analogy: Trainers conditioning players, equipment managers altering jerseys and boxing shipments, and a cleanup crew hauling trash

enemy.name: Trash-Talk Tackle
enemy.taunt: I'll flatten your proteins and trash your organelles!

subtopics.name: Powerhouse Drive: Mitochondria and Plant Specials
subtopics.lesson: Mitochondria are the stadium generators, carrying out cellular respiration to turn glucose and oxygen into ATP, and they even carry their own DNA. Plant teams play on a reinforced home field with extra structures. They add a cellulose cell wall for support, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a large central vacuole.
subtopics.analogy: Stadium generators powering night games plus a home stadium with extra walls, solar panels, and a water tower

enemy.name: Powerhouse Punter
enemy.taunt: My generator legs will punt your ATP into the stands!

subtopics.name: Goal-Line Defense: Membrane and Transport
subtopics.lesson: The plasma membrane is like stadium gates, a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins that is selectively permeable. Fans slipping from crowded to empty sections without energy mirror passive transport by diffusion, osmosis, and facilitated diffusion down the concentration gradient. Hauling gear uphill with extra energy mirrors active transport, which uses ATP to move substances against their gradient, like the sodium-potassium pump.
subtopics.analogy: Stadium gates with security staff deciding entry, with fans drifting in freely versus staff carrying coolers uphill with extra energy

enemy.name: Shutdown Corner
enemy.taunt: Nothing crosses my membrane without my permission!

cs:fantasy.title: Knights of the Data Keep
cs:fantasy.overview: Enter the Data Keep, where knights and dragons guard ancient structures of power. To claim the throne you must master arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, and search trees. Learn how each structure trades speed for order in battle.
cs:fantasy.summary: Arrays give instant O(1) reads but costly O(n) middle inserts, while linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, and balanced trees each optimize for different access patterns. Big-O ties them together by describing how running time grows with input size.
cs:fantasy.limitation: Castles and dragons make the trade-offs memorable, but real contiguous memory, pointers, hash functions, and tree balance involve no magic or bravery, and Big-O ignores constant factors that can still matter in real code.

boss.name: Dragon King Malachar
boss.intro: I have hoarded every array, list, and tree in the realm — defeat me and prove you are the true master of data!

subtopics.name: Arrays
subtopics.lesson: Like shields hung in contiguous slots, an array stores elements in contiguous memory so a knight can grab any shield by its number instantly in O(1) time. Slipping a new shield into the middle forces every shield after it to shift down, which takes O(n) work. Arrays are best when you need fast reading by index and rarely insert in the middle.
subtopics.analogy: A solid shield-wall where each shield hangs side-by-side in numbered slots along the castle wall

enemy.name: Shield-Wall Orc
enemy.taunt: Try to pierce my unbroken line, little knight!

subtopics.name: Linked Lists
subtopics.lesson: Like knights each pointing to the next scout, a linked list stores nodes that each hold a value and a pointer to the next node. If a knight already knows his neighbor, slipping a new ally in right after him is O(1) with no shifting. But finding a distant knight means following pointers one by one, so search is O(n).
subtopics.analogy: A dragon-hunt chain where each knight holds a lantern and points to the next knight in the dark forest

enemy.name: Cave Troll Lurker
enemy.taunt: Follow my endless chain if you dare, knight!

subtopics.name: Stacks and Queues
subtopics.lesson: Like piling quest plates where you push and pop only the top plate, a stack is last-in, first-out with O(1) push and pop, powering the call stack and undo spells. Like knights queuing at the gate, a queue is first-in, first-out where you enqueue at the back and dequeue at the front, powering breadth-first search and printer queues. One rewards the newest arrival, the other honors the oldest.
subtopics.analogy: A stack of enchanted feast plates versus a line of knights waiting at the drawbridge gate

enemy.name: Gatekeeper Wraith
enemy.taunt: Only the worthy pass in order — choose poorly and perish!

subtopics.name: Hash Tables
subtopics.lesson: Like a vault rune that maps each hero name to an alcove number, a hash table uses a hash function to map keys to array indices for average O(1) insert, lookup and delete. When two names point to the same alcove, the collision is handled by chaining or open addressing. When the vault grows crowded, the table resizes when the load factor gets too high.
subtopics.analogy: A dragon vault where a magic rune instantly tells which numbered alcove holds each named treasure chest

enemy.name: Vault Mimic
enemy.taunt: Your key will never find its lock in my shifting vault!

subtopics.name: Binary Search Trees and Big-O
subtopics.lesson: Like sorting dragons so smaller drakes roost left and larger drakes roost right of each elder, a binary search tree keeps smaller keys on the left and larger keys on the right. When the tree is balanced, search, insert and delete are O(log n), but when it stretches into a line they degrade to O(n). Big-O itself describes how running time grows with input size, ignoring constant factors.
subtopics.analogy: A branching dragon family tree where younger wyrmlings perch left and elder drakes perch right of each elder

enemy.name: Crooked Branch Dragon
enemy.taunt: My branches twist — balance them if you can, knight!

econ:fantasy.title: Dragonhold Markets
econ:fantasy.overview: Enter the Dragonhold bazaar where knights haggle for swords, potions, and saddles. Learn how supply and demand set prices, how shifting tastes and kingly decrees disrupt equilibrium, and how buyers and sellers count their spoils.
econ:fantasy.summary: Equilibrium price balances what buyers want and sellers offer, while shifts, elasticity, and price controls explain how that balance changes or breaks. Consumer and producer surplus show the gains buyers and sellers keep from trading at the market price.
econ:fantasy.limitation: The knight-and-dragon bazaar makes curves feel like duels, but real markets are models not battlefields: willingness to pay and sellers' costs cannot be seen like health bars, and price ceilings and floors play out through shortages and surpluses not dragon fire.

boss.name: Dragon Empress of Markets
boss.intro: You balanced petty stalls, but now face my flames — I am the final reckoning of supply and demand!

subtopics.name: Law of Demand
subtopics.lesson: Demand shows how much buyers want at each price. In the bazaar, when the enchanted potion price climbs higher, knights cut back and save their gold, so quantity demanded falls as price rises. That inverse link is the law of demand every adventurer must respect.
subtopics.analogy: Haggling for healing potions as prices rise in a dragon-guarded bazaar

enemy.name: Potion Scalper
enemy.taunt: Want to heal, tin-can? Then pay my price!

subtopics.name: Supply and Equilibrium
subtopics.lesson: Supply shows how much sellers offer at each price, and higher sword prices coax blacksmiths to forge more blades. When the knights' desire meets the smiths' offers, the supply and demand curves cross at market equilibrium. There quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, settling the battle over price.
subtopics.analogy: Blacksmiths forging more swords when castle prices rise to meet knights at equilibrium

enemy.name: Forge Troll
enemy.taunt: More gold, more steel — cross my bridge if you can!

subtopics.name: Shifts vs Movements
subtopics.lesson: Not all changes are the same in the quest market. If quest rewards raise incomes, bards change tastes, or the price of a related good moves, the whole demand curve shifts and changes the equilibrium price and quantity. If only the good's own price changes, knights simply move along the same curve to a new quantity.
subtopics.analogy: Quest gold, bard songs, and rival gear shifting a knight's desire for armor

enemy.name: Charm Bard
enemy.taunt: I change hearts and purses — try to keep up, knight!

subtopics.name: Price Elasticity of Demand
subtopics.lesson: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to price. Luxury dragon jewels with many substitutes are elastic and vanish from carts when prices rise. Life-saving remedies like insulin and short-run gasoline are inelastic and knights keep buying them even when prices climb.
subtopics.analogy: Choosing between luxury dragon gems and life-saving elixirs when prices change

enemy.name: Elastic Dragon
enemy.taunt: Stretch your coin purse or burn, little knight!

subtopics.name: Price Controls and Surplus
subtopics.lesson: When the king sets a price ceiling below equilibrium like rent control, brave tenants find too few rooms and a shortage grips the town. When he sets a price floor above equilibrium like a minimum wage, a surplus of labor waits unhired. Even at a fair market price, trade creates spoils: consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers are willing to pay and what they actually pay. Producer surplus is the gap between the price and the sellers' costs.
subtopics.analogy: A king decreeing rents and squire wages while knights and smiths count their spoils

enemy.name: Crown Tyrant
enemy.taunt: I decree the prices — let them face shortage and surplus!

econ:sports.title: Gridiron Markets
econ:sports.overview: Welcome to Gridiron Markets, where every snap is a battle between supply and demand. You will call plays with ticket prices, fan demand, and vendor supply to find the winning equilibrium. Master market forces to march downfield and lift the championship trophy.
econ:sports.summary: Demand falls as price rises while supply rises with price, and they meet at market equilibrium where quantity supplied equals quantity demanded. Shifts, elasticity, and price controls explain how that balance moves or breaks, while consumer and producer surplus measure who gains from the trade.
econ:sports.limitation: Football has fixed downs, referees, and a final whistle, while real markets have continuous prices and curves that can shift from many income, taste, and related-good changes at once.

boss.name: Commissioner Blitz
boss.intro: I set the caps, the floors, and the rules of this entire league — break my market defense if you want the title!

subtopics.name: Law of Demand
subtopics.lesson: In a football ticket market, demand means how much buyers want at each possible price. The law of demand says that as price rises, quantity demanded falls because fewer fans are willing to pay. Like a stadium filling up only when prices drop, buyers want more at low prices and less at high prices.
subtopics.analogy: Scrambling for cheap nosebleed seats versus pricey 50-yard-line tickets on game day

enemy.name: Lockdown Corner
enemy.taunt: No bargain completions in my coverage, rookie!

subtopics.name: Supply and Equilibrium
subtopics.lesson: Supply is how much sellers offer at each price, with quantity supplied rising as price rises because selling becomes more profitable. When higher prices bring more goods from sellers but less interest from buyers, the two sides meet at market equilibrium. That is the price where the supply and demand curves cross and quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.
subtopics.analogy: Vendors deciding how much gear to hawk as prices climb toward kickoff

enemy.name: Trench Tackle
enemy.taunt: You shall not cross my line of scrimmage!

subtopics.name: Shifts vs. Moves
subtopics.lesson: A change in a ticket's own price just moves fans along the same demand curve to a different quantity demanded. But if fan tastes surge after a winning season, if incomes rise, or if the price of a related good changes, the whole demand curve shifts. That shift changes both the equilibrium price and equilibrium quantity where supply and demand meet.
subtopics.analogy: A star quarterback signing suddenly packing the stands even at the same ticket prices

enemy.name: Bandwagon Fans
enemy.taunt: We only show up when it's trendy — try to predict us!

subtopics.name: Elasticity of Demand
subtopics.lesson: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly quantity demanded responds to a price change. Demand is elastic when buyers respond a lot, as with luxuries and goods that have many substitutes. It is inelastic when buyers respond little, like insulin or gasoline in the short run where buyers have few alternatives.
subtopics.analogy: Fans skipping pricey luxury suites but still buying gas for the road trip no matter the cost

enemy.name: Stretch Receiver
enemy.taunt: I bend a lot or a little — guess how I'll react!

subtopics.name: Controls and Surplus
subtopics.lesson: A price ceiling set below equilibrium, like rent control, keeps price low and causes a shortage because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. A price floor set above equilibrium, like a minimum wage, keeps price high and can cause a surplus. At the market price, consumer surplus is the gap between what buyers were willing to pay and what they pay, while producer surplus is the gap between the price and sellers' costs.
subtopics.analogy: League-capped ticket prices leaving fans in line and guaranteed concession pay leaving unsold hot dogs

enemy.name: Flag-Happy Ref
enemy.taunt: I throw caps and floors on every play — deal with it!

hist:sports.title: Gridiron WWII
hist:sports.overview: Welcome to Gridiron WWII, where World War II plays out like a hard-fought football season. You will call defensive stops from appeasement to Blitzkrieg and lead comeback drives from Stalingrad to Normandy. Master the real history from Versailles in 1919 to surrender in 1945 to win the title.
hist:sports.summary: Resentment over Versailles and appeasement in the 1930s let Germany launch Blitzkrieg and expand the war, while defeat in the Battle of Britain and at Stalingrad halted that momentum. The United States entered after Pearl Harbor and Allied landings in Normandy opened the final drive that ended with German surrender in May 1945 and Japanese surrender in August 1945 after Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
hist:sports.limitation: Football is a timed game with referees, penalties, and second chances, while World War II involved real invasion, occupation, and atomic bombings with no rulebook or replay, so talk of yardage and comebacks cannot capture the human cost from Poland to Pearl Harbor to Normandy.

boss.name: Gridiron Overlord
boss.intro: It's championship overtime from Versailles to Hiroshima — beat me or history rewrites itself!

subtopics.name: Versailles Fallout
subtopics.lesson: Like a team punished after a big loss, Germany was blamed for World War I under the 1919 Treaty of Versailles, stripped of territory and ordered to pay heavy reparations. That harsh penalty call fueled deep resentment in the locker room. During the Great Depression that anger helped the Nazi Party gain support.
subtopics.analogy: A championship loser hit with a brutal penalty — huge yardage taken away and a massive fine that leaves the whole locker room furious.

enemy.name: Penalty Flag
enemy.taunt: You broke the rules in 1919 — now pay the yards, chump!

subtopics.name: Appeasement Drive
subtopics.lesson: Like coaches playing prevent defense and refusing to tackle, Britain and France followed appeasement in the 1930s. They let Hitler remilitarize the Rhineland and annex Austria without a stop. At the Munich Conference in 1938 they let him take the Sudetenland, giving up more field instead of forcing a turnover.
subtopics.analogy: A soft defense that keeps giving up free yards hoping the opposing offense will stop attacking on its own.

enemy.name: Soft Coach
enemy.taunt: Take another 15 yards — I just want a friendly game!

subtopics.name: Blitzkrieg and Britain's Air Stand
subtopics.lesson: Like a hurry-up offense using every weapon at once, Blitzkrieg combined tanks, aircraft and fast infantry to overwhelm defenses. That fast drive knocked France out in just six weeks in 1940 after Germany invaded Poland on September 1, 1939 and Britain and France declared war. Then the game went entirely to the air, where the RAF beat back Germany in the Battle of Britain and stopped an invasion.
subtopics.analogy: A no-huddle lightning offense that shreds the line, followed by an all-air showdown with no ground game at all.

enemy.name: Blitz Backer
enemy.taunt: Lightning rush coming — your line will collapse in six weeks!

subtopics.name: Eastern Freeze and Pacific Shock
subtopics.lesson: Like an overconfident road team marching into a blizzard, Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941. The home team held the line at Stalingrad in 1943, and that stop turned the tide in the east. In a separate stadium, Japan's attack on Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941 pulled the United States into the war.
subtopics.analogy: A goal-line stand in freezing snow that flips momentum, while a surprise cheap shot in another stadium drags a new powerhouse team into the tournament.

enemy.name: Snow Bowl Bruiser
enemy.taunt: Come into my frozen end zone and you'll never leave!

subtopics.name: D-Day to Final Whistle
subtopics.lesson: Like a final two-minute drill, Allied forces landed in Normandy on D-Day, June 6, 1944 and opened a western front. That drive closed out one side when Germany surrendered in May 1945. The other side tapped out when Japan surrendered in August 1945 after the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
subtopics.analogy: A massive fourth-quarter comeback drive starting deep in your own territory that ends with both opposing teams tapping out.

enemy.name: Hail Mary Hero
enemy.taunt: I'm throwing deep from Normandy — try to stop this final drive!

photo:sports.title: Gridiron Photosynthesis Blitz
photo:sports.overview: Welcome to the Photosynthesis Bowl, where every leaf is a stadium turning bright lights into championship points. You will run light-powered drives, execute a carbon-fixing comeback, and manage your gates to stockpile glucose. Master light, water, and air to outscore the darkness.
photo:sports.summary: Light-dependent reactions in the thylakoid membranes split water to release oxygen and store energy in ATP and NADPH after chlorophyll captures red and blue light. In the stroma RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide entering through stomata, using that stored energy to build glucose, while light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature limit the rate.
photo:sports.limitation: A football game is decided by play-calling, huddles, and scoring drives, while photosynthesis is chemistry driven by light, water splitting, enzymes like RuBisCO, and gas diffusion, so gates, tackles and scoreboards do not capture how stomata trade water loss or how ATP and NADPH power sugar formation.

boss.intro: In scorching heat with the gates slammed shut, the undefeated champions starve your offense of air and water for one final stand!

subtopics.name: The Championship Formula
subtopics.lesson: Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose. The full play is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light yields C6H12O6 + 6O2. The whole game is played inside chloroplasts, which serve as stadiums for this conversion.

subtopics.name: Light-Dependent Blitz
subtopics.lesson: The light-dependent reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes. There chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light, water is split and oxygen is released. The captured energy is stored in ATP and NADPH to power later steps.
subtopics.analogy: A fast no-huddle drive under bright stadium lights where the line bursts through to bank energy for later

enemy.name: Thylakoid Tackler
enemy.taunt: I'm hitting you in the trenches where the lights burn brightest!

subtopics.name: Calvin Cycle Comeback
subtopics.lesson: The Calvin cycle takes place in the stroma of the chloroplast. There the enzyme RuBisCO fixes carbon dioxide. ATP and NADPH from the light reactions then turn that fixed carbon into sugar.
subtopics.analogy: A methodical fourth-quarter comeback drive that cashes in earlier momentum to put points on the board

subtopics.name: Stomata Defense and Field Conditions
subtopics.lesson: Stomata on leaves let carbon dioxide in and oxygen out, but they also lose water. Plants close them in hot, dry weather to save water. Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature all limit how fast photosynthesis runs.
subtopics.analogy: Stadium gates opening for fans and fresh air but closing in extreme heat, with lights, crowd size and temperature controlling game speed

enemy.name: Drought Cornerback

algo:fantasy.title: Dragonkeep: Algorithm Quest
algo:fantasy.overview: Welcome to Dragonkeep, where knights master algorithms to outwit dragons and conquer dungeons. You will wield heaps, graphs, searches, and sorts like swords and spells to find shortest paths and hidden treasure.
algo:fantasy.summary: Priority queues built on heaps power Dijkstra on weighted roads, while queues power BFS on unweighted roads and stacks power DFS. Hash maps offer instant finds unless collisions strike, and merge sort stays steady while quicksort risks its worst case.
algo:fantasy.limitation: Castles, dragons, and vaults make the ideas vivid, but real structures are abstract code with exact costs like O(log n) and O(1), and their guarantees depend on completeness, non-negative weights, hash quality, and stability, not bravery.

boss.name: Morgath the Algorithm Dragon
boss.intro: Face me, knight, for I guard every path, heap, and spell — only a true master of algorithms shall claim my hoard!

subtopics.name: Min-Heaps and Priority Queues
subtopics.lesson: A min-heap is a complete binary tree where every parent is smaller than its children, like a ranking where each captain outranks those below. Insert and remove-min both cost O(log n) as knights shuffle up or down the pyramid. Heaps are the engine behind priority queues, always handing you the smallest, most urgent quest first.
subtopics.analogy: A tournament lineup where the weakest squire always stands at the front of a perfectly filled pyramid of knights.

enemy.name: Heap Troll
enemy.taunt: My ranks are chaos — find your precious minimum if you can!

subtopics.name: Graphs and Their Scrolls
subtopics.lesson: A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges, like castles joined by roads. Knights record it as an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix, two different ways to store the same connections. The choice is only about storage, not about changing the castles and roads themselves.

subtopics.name: Breadth-First and Depth-First Scouts
subtopics.lesson: Breadth-first search uses a queue and finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs, sweeping outward like a torch line advancing together. Depth-first search instead uses a stack or recursion, plunging down one path like a lone knight before backtracking. Only breadth-first search promises the shortest path when all steps cost the same.
subtopics.analogy: Sending squires to sweep a dungeon level by level versus sending one knight deep down a single tunnel.

enemy.name: Dungeon Knight
enemy.taunt: Level by level or deep and dark? Choose wrong and you are lost forever!

subtopics.name: Dijkstra's Dragon Paths
subtopics.lesson: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths when edges have non-negative weights, like roads with different travel costs but no cursed shortcuts. It uses a priority queue to always expand the closest unvisited stronghold next. If weights were negative, its promise would no longer hold.
subtopics.analogy: A dragon weighing mountain passes to hoard the fastest route between keeps.

enemy.name: Ember Dragon
enemy.taunt: These weighted roads are mine — pay the toll or perish on the long way!

subtopics.name: Hash Map Treasure Vaults
subtopics.lesson: Hash maps give average O(1) lookups, letting a knight grab treasure almost instantly. A bad hash function causes many collisions, forcing many items into the same chest. Then lookups degrade to O(n) worst-case as you must rummage through everything piled together.
subtopics.analogy: A vault where each treasure's name magically points to its chest.

enemy.name: Vault Hydra
enemy.taunt: One key, a hundred chests — let's see you find anything now!

subtopics.name: Merge Sort vs Quicksort Duels
subtopics.lesson: Merge sort runs in O(n log n) and is stable, keeping equal knights in their original order. Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but falls to O(n squared) in the worst case when its choices go badly. One is steady, the other is usually fast but can stumble.

cells2:fantasy.title: Dragon Cell Keep
